description:
Team made by current first year undergraduate students at the University of Warwick studying Robotics Engineering with AI (first time hackathons for many).

Looking to take anyone who can help work through multidisciplinary roles and aid team members when help is needed.
summary:
Ever wondered what it takes to bring astronauts home from another world? In Orbital Uprise, players become aerospace engineers at Mission Control and design a round trip to a real exoplanet, guided by CAPCOM Cass, a friendly robot.

Our project addresses the challenge by making mission trade-offs feel real. Players pick engines, fuel tanks, a deep-space drive, an antenna, a pressure system and a heat shield, all within a budget. Adding crew multiplies the score on a successful flight but costs points on a failed one, and better parts cost more.

Players learn by trying, failing and redesigning. Mid-flight, they face black holes, asteroid swarms, solar flares and quasars, escaping each with a timed science quiz or mini-game. After every flight, a mission report explains in real numbers why it succeeded or failed. Planet data comes from the NASA Exoplanet Archive.

As a result, students build intuition for engineering trade-offs while having fun. The game has three difficulty levels, collectable badges, a splashdown celebration, a leaderboard for each 3-launch run, and sound effects with a space soundtrack.
details:
What it does

  • You are a new NASA rocket engineer.
  • Pick a real exoplanet (19 to choose from).
  • Build a rocket that can get there and back.
  • Stay within your budget.
  • Launch and watch a hand-drawn cutscene of your flight.
  • Escape space hazards on the way: black holes, aliens, asteroids, debris, quasars, solar flares and strong gravity.
  • Beat each hazard with a quick quiz or a mini-game, against the clock.
  • Read a mission report that explains why your flight worked or failed.
  • Earn badges and post your 3-launch average to the leaderboard.

Benefits

  • You learn by trying, failing and fixing.
  • Planet data comes from the NASA Exoplanet Archive.
  • It uses real rocket physics, simplified for players.
  • Every number is labelled as NASA data or a game assumption.
  • Quiz answers link to NASA sources.
  • It’s free, runs in a browser and works on phones.
  • It’s accessible: keyboard controls, captions, a Calm mode and bigger text.

Intended impact

  • Show students that space missions are about trade-offs.
  • More fuel means more weight.
  • Better parts cost more.
  • Taking a crew means bigger rewards but bigger risks.
  • Getting home matters as much as getting there.
  • Spark curiosity about exoplanets and engineering.

Tools we used

  • TypeScript, React and Vite
  • Tailwind CSS and Motion for the design and animation
  • Howler.js and the Web Audio API for sound
  • Python scripts to generate the sound effects
  • ffmpeg to build the cutscene videos
  • NASA Exoplanet Archive for planet data
  • Vitest and Playwright for testing
  • GitHub Pages for hosting
  • Claude Code, an AI assistant, to help write and test the code
  • No special hardware, just a laptop and a browser

What makes it creative

  • Cutscenes hand-drawn by our artist
  • The rocket’s look changes with the parts you choose
  • The flight pauses mid-air for surprise dangers
  • You choose your way out: answer a question or play a game
  • Sticker-book Mission Control style with pixel-art scenes
  • The alien ship is clearly marked “just for fun”

What we considered

  • Keeping the science honest while making it fun
  • Three levels for different ages: Cadet, Engineer and Flight Director
  • Random hazards that get harder each launch
  • Accessibility for all players
  • Small video files so it works on slow internet
  • Being honest about limits: the live leaderboard saves scores on each player’s own device
